name: Catoca
description: Large kimberlite mine in Lunda Sul; Endiama 59%, Omani investor 41% since 2024

name: Argyle
description: Rio Tinto, 1985–2020; supplied over 90% of the world’s pink diamonds

name: Jwaneng
description: Debswana open pit, opened 1982; mining at about 452 m and planned to reach 816 m by 2034

name: Karowe
description: Lucara open pit on the AK6 pipe, producing since 2012; source of the 1,109 ct Lesedi La Rona (2015) and the 2,488 ct Motswedi (2024)
notes: Coordinate stated by the operator.

name: Orapa
description: Debswana mine opened in 1971; largest diamond mine by area
notes: “Largest by area” is the operator’s own characterization.

name: Diavik
description: Rio Tinto mine under Lac de Gras; final production March 2026 after more than 150 million ct

name: Ekati
description: Canada’s first diamond mine (1998); receivership on 14 July 2026 ended mining as a going concern; wind-down of about five weeks, now care and maintenance
notes: In care and maintenance under a court-appointed receiver; no permanent closure declared as of 15 September 2026.

name: Gahcho Kué
description: De Beers 51%, Mountain Province 49%; opened 2016, production expected to end in late 2027

name: Mbuji-Mayi
description: Kasai diamond fields developed by MIBA; widely worked by artisanal diggers

name: Kollur (Golconda workings)
description: Alluvial workings of the Golconda group on the Krishna; Indian output peaked in the 1600s, and Brazilian finds of the early 1700s ended its lead
notes: Mindat’s point for the Kollur Mine, about 2 km north of the Krishna, while the workings are described on the south bank.

name: Letseng
description: Gem Diamonds 70%, Lesotho 30%; the highest diamond mine at about 3,100 m, worked for large high-value stones

name: Namibian marine fields
description: Debmarine Namibia’s Atlantic 1 license; seabed gravels mined at 90–140 m depth (approximate center)
notes: Estimated center of the Atlantic 1 license area. The 90–140 m mining depth is not confirmed from a primary source.

name: Jubilee (Yubileynaya)
description: Alrosa open pit about 20 km from Aikhal, Yakutia

name: Mir
description: Alrosa pipe at Mirny, Yakutia; open pit ended 2001, underground mine flooded in 2017; a separate deeper mine is being sunk on the site
notes: Mining has not resumed. A separate, deeper mine is being sunk on the site; its timetable rests on news wires, so no date is given.

name: Udachny
description: Alrosa pipe in Yakutia; open pit about 640 m deep, now mined underground

name: Koidu
description: Kimberlite mine in Kono district; operations halted in 2025 after a labor dispute
notes: The 2025 halt rests on a trade-press report (MINING.COM), the chapter’s only trade-press source.

name: Cullinan
description: Petra Diamonds; source of the 3,106.75 ct Cullinan diamond (1905)

name: Finsch
description: Petra Diamonds kimberlite mine at Lime Acres, Northern Cape; in business rescue, production suspended on 10 June 2026
notes: The Lime Acres point. In business rescue, production suspended on 10 June 2026. The chapter has no separate citation for this yet.

name: Kimberley (Big Hole)
description: Worked 1871–1914 to 240 m; about 14.5 million ct recovered

name: Venetia
description: De Beers mine in Limpopo; moved from open pit to underground mining

name: Williamson (Mwadui)
description: Mwadui pipe, about 146 ha at surface; source of the Williamson Pink (1947); Petra sold its stake in May 2025
notes: Production after Petra’s May 2025 sale is not confirmed by an institutional source.

name: Marange (Chiadzwa)
description: Diamonds in weathered Umkondo conglomerate, rushed from 2006; operators folded into the state company ZCDC in 2016
notes: Chiadzwa point. “Active” rests on ZCDC’s own description of its operations.

name: Anakie gemfields
description: Central Queensland alluvial field around Sapphire, Rubyvale and Anakie

name: Pailin
description: Gem fields once a leading sapphire source; exploited by the Khmer Rouge

name: Kashmir (Padar)
description: Mines at about 4,600 m near Sumjam; main output 1882–1887 (point marks the Padar District)
notes: Padar District point, not the Sumjam mine.

name: Ilakaka
description: Alluvial sapphire rush after a 1998 discovery

name: Montepuez
description: Gemfields 75%, Mwiriti 25%; 33,600 ha concession near Montepuez town, mining since 2012
notes: Town point; the mine lies to the east.

name: Mogok
description: The classic ruby district; held by TNLA rebels from July 2024 to October 2025

name: Mong Hsu
description: Shan State, about 250 km southeast of Mogok; marble-hosted ruby with violet cores, on the Bangkok market from 1992
notes: Township node. Current output is undocumented; “artisanal” is a judgment.

name: Ratnapura
description: Gem gravels worked from hand-dug pits 10–50 m deep

name: Chanthaburi
description: Basalt-related gem gravels, now far less productive; major gem-trading town
notes: Its role as a current trading center is unverified.

name: Yogo Gulch
description: Montana; unheated cornflower-blue sapphire mined from 1895, now mostly hobby mining

name: Luc Yen
description: Yen Bai province; gems found in placers in 1987 and mined from 1988, now worked by small groups of local miners
notes: District centroid.

name: Panjshir Valley (Khenj)
description: Informal mines at about 2,100–4,400 m; the village of Khenj lies about 113 km northeast of Kabul
notes: The chapter’s editorial record gives elevations of about 2,100 to 4,300 m from GIA (Spring 1991); the description here says 4,400 m.

name: Belmont
description: Open pit and underground mine 13 km southeast of Itabira, worked since 1978; the largest colored-stone operation in Minas Gerais
notes: Computed from Itabira plus the 13 km southeast that GIA gives.

name: Chivor
description: Reached by the Spanish in 1537, abandoned, and reopened in the late 19th century

name: Coscuez
description: Emerald district in San Pablo de Borbur municipality, western Boyacá

name: Muzo
description: Western Boyacá; worked by the Muzo people before the Spanish, who took over from the 1540s

name: Shakiso
description: Emeralds mined near Kenticha reached world markets in late 2016 (point marks the trading town)
notes: Trading town, not the mines near Kenticha.

name: Swat valley (Mingora)
description: Emerald in talc-carbonate rock of the Indus suture; Mingora opened in 1958, with Gujar Kili now the leading producer

name: Malysheva (Mariinsky mine)
description: Mine in the Ural emerald belt at Malyshevo; emerald and alexandrite come from the same schists, worked since the 1830s
notes: Town node from OpenStreetMap (Nominatim).

name: Kagem
description: Open pit in the Ndola Rural Emerald Restricted Area, Copperbelt; Gemfields 75%, IDC 25%

name: Sar-e-Sang
description: Kokcha valley, Badakhshan; lapis source of the ancient world

name: Coober Pedy
description: South Australia; opal found in 1915, more than 70 opal fields

name: Lightning Ridge
description: New South Wales black opal field; first shafts sunk in 1905

name: Capão mine (Ouro Preto)
description: Minas Gerais; mechanised mine 3 km west of Rodrigo Silva, in the Ouro Preto district, the only known source of imperial topaz since the 1700s
notes: Rodrigo Silva node from OpenStreetMap (Nominatim), moved 3 km west, the distance GIA gives. “Active” is judged, not sourced; the newest institutional confirmation is GIA, Winter 1996.

name: São José da Batalha
description: Source of the first Paraíba tourmaline, which reached the gem market in 1989 (approximate location)

name: Teófilo Otoni district
description: Gem-trading city for the pegmatite fields of northeastern Minas Gerais

name: Zabargad (St John’s Island)
description: Red Sea island 3.2 by 2.4 km, worked for peridot since antiquity; commercial mining ran from about 1906 until nationalisation in 1958
notes: Coordinate printed by Gems & Gemology (Spring 1981); good to about 0.01 degrees. “Historic” rather than “closed”: nationalised in 1958 and later abandoned, with no closing date recorded.

name: Wegel Tena (Wollo)
description: Precious opal found in 2008 in volcanic rock at about 3,000 m, worked from hand-dug tunnels by crews of 10 to 20 miners

name: Motagua valley
description: The Mesoamerican jadeite source, rediscovered in 1952; jadeitite runs about 110 km along the north side of the valley, Baja Verapaz to Zacapa
notes: Usumatlán node from OpenStreetMap (Nominatim), a district point on the north side of the valley. “Artisanal” is judged, not sourced.

name: Nishapur turquoise mines
description: Ancient mines at Ma’dan, about 50 km northwest of Nishapur, still worked

name: Ago Bay
description: Mie prefecture; Mikimoto’s experiments began here about 1890 and produced the first cultured pearls in 1893
notes: Bay center about 2 km southwest of Kashikojima, from OpenStreetMap (Nominatim). “Active” is judged, not sourced, from continued Japanese akoya output.

name: Hpakant
description: Kachin State; the world’s main source of gem jadeite, worked in open pits through boulder-bearing conglomerate

name: Yantarny (Primorskoye)
description: Kaliningrad amber combine; open pit worked since 1976 on the largest known amber deposit, 627 t produced in 2024

name: Mahenge (Epanko)
description: Pinkish red spinel crystals up to 54 kg found at Epanko in August 2007, a few kilometers southwest of Mahenge town

name: Merelani Hills
description: Only commercial tanzanite source, about 7 × 2 km, enclosed by a 24 km wall
